summary: This FYI memo is a catalog of tools for monitoring and debugging TCP/IP networks and connected devices, updating the earlier FYI 2 in RFC 1147. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: This is a tool shop catalog for people who fix networks, listing programs that help find problems.

questions: how to submit a tool to the noctools catalog
subtitle: A June 1993 catalog of tools for watching, testing and debugging TCP/IP networks, with a standard entry format and a keyword index.

tldr.problem: People who run networks need to know which tools exist for monitoring and debugging TCP/IP internets, but a printed list goes out of date as soon as new tools appear.
tldr.mechanism: The NOCtools2 Working Group compiled one catalog in which every tool has an entry in the same template (name, keywords, abstract, mechanism, caveats, bugs, limitations, requirements, availability), plus a keyword index so tools can be compared.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1470 is an Informational update of FYI 2 (RFC 1147) and says it replaces that memo. The authors point readers to an on-line version for current entries and state that the IETF does not endorse any listed tool.

today: RFC 1470 is an Informational memo that obsoletes RFC 1147, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The memo itself says its entries may be out of date and sends readers to the on-line catalog for current information.

sections.title: Why a Tool Catalog
sections.content:
RFC 1470 is FYI 2, an update to the earlier catalog in RFC 1147. Its goal is to give site administrators and network managers practical information about tools for monitoring and debugging TCP/IP internets and interconnected devices. New and updated tools are listed in this edition.

The editors admit that a static document cannot hold references to the latest tools or recent revisions to older entries. So the NOCtools catalog is also available on-line, through the Usenet newsgroup comp.networks.noctools and by anonymous FTP from wuarchive.wustl.edu in the directory /doc/noctools. Because of publication delays, some entries in the RFC may be out of date, and readers are urged to consult the on-line service.

The catalog was compiled by the NOCTools2 Working Group of the IETF User Services Area. The memo names Chris Myers, Darren Kinley, Gary Malkin, Mohamed Ellozy and Mike Patton as especially notable contributors.

The IETF does not endorse any tool in the catalog. For the most part the editors neither evaluated the tools nor validated their descriptions, and most descriptions of commercial tools were supplied by vendors. The memo's own advice is Caveat Emptor.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a list of helper programs for fixing networks. Because new helpers keep showing up, the list also lives online, and the authors say not to trust any helper just because it is on the list.

sections.title: The Standard Entry Template
sections.content:
Every tool is described in the same format so that tools can be compared. The template begins with NAME, followed by the tool's KEYWORDS, and then these sections: ABSTRACT, MECHANISM, CAVEATS, BUGS, LIMITATIONS, HARDWARE REQUIRED, SOFTWARE REQUIRED, AVAILABILITY AND CONTACT POINT FOR INFORMATION ABOUT THIS TOOL, CONTACT POINT FOR CHANGES TO THIS CATALOG ENTRY and DATE OF MOST RECENT UPDATE TO THIS CATALOG ENTRY (written as YYMMDD).

The tool descriptions explain the roles. The ABSTRACT gives a detailed description of a tool's purpose and characteristics. The MECHANISM says how it works. CAVEATS hold warnings about use, BUGS hold known bugs or bug-report procedures, and LIMITATIONS describe the boundaries of what the tool can do. The hardware and software sections give the operating environment, and the availability section points to vendors, on-line repositories or other sources.

Where two tools share a name, the vendor name is added. For example, MITRE and SNMP Research each submitted a tool called NETMON, so the catalog lists them as NETMON_MITRE and NETMON_WINDOWS_SNMP_RESEARCH.
sections.plainLanguage: Every tool gets the same form to fill in, like a trading card with boxes for what it does, how it works, what can go wrong and where to find it. That way you can compare cards side by side.

sections.title: Keywords for Comparing Tools
sections.content:
Keywords are terse, abbreviated attributes of a tool or its use. They are always listed in a predefined order, sorted first by category and then alphabetically. There are five categories: the general management area or functional role, the network resources or components being managed, the mechanism the tool uses, the operating system and hardware environment, and the tool's characteristics as a hardware or software acquisition.

Examples of functional roles include Alarm (a reporting or logging tool that can trigger on specific events), Analyzer (a traffic monitor that reconstructs and interprets protocol messages spanning several packets), Debugger, Generator (a traffic generation tool), Map, Routing and Security. Resource keywords name what is managed, such as DNS, Ethernet, FDDI, IP, NFS, OSI and SMTP.

Mechanism keywords include Eavesdrop (silently monitoring a medium, for example by putting an ethernet interface into promiscuous mode), Ping (sending probes such as ICMP echo messages), SNMP, RMON, CMIS, Spoof (testing a remote protocol module by peer-level message exchange) and Curses. Environment keywords include DOS, UNIX, VMS, Macintosh, OS/2 and Standalone, and acquisition keywords include Free, Library and Sourcelib.
sections.plainLanguage: Keywords are like stickers on each tool card, such as 'works on UNIX' or 'free'. You can look for every tool with the same sticker.

sections.title: The Keyword Index
sections.content:
Right after the keyword definitions comes an index titled Tools Indexed by Keywords. It lists, under each keyword, the tools that carry it, with keywords and tool names both in alphabetical order. The index reflects the contents of the on-line documentation, and the on-line version is where the most up-to-date index lives (the memo gives the newsgroup comp.networks.noctools.tools and an FTP directory).

For example, the Alarm list includes NOCOL, LanProbe and LANWatch, while the Analyzer list includes LANVista, PacketView, Sniffer and SpiderMonitor. The Benchmark list holds tools such as spray, ttcp and iozone. The index lets a reader jump from a need, such as 'something that benchmarks NFS', to candidate tools and then to their entries.

The tool entries themselves follow in alphabetical order by tool name, each headed 'Internet Tool Catalog' with the tool's identifier.
sections.plainLanguage: The index is like the back of a cookbook: instead of reading every recipe, you look up the word you care about and it tells you which cards to read.

sections.title: Classic Diagnostic Tools in the Catalog
sections.content:
Many entries describe small, familiar tools. arp displays and can modify the internet-to-ethernet address translation tables used by the address resolution protocol; only the super user can modify ARP entries. netstat reads kernel data structures and reports on the routing table, TCP connections, TCP and UDP 'listens' and protocol memory management. nslookup is an interactive front end to the BIND resolver routines for querying DNS servers, and DiG (domain information groper) was written to be more convenient and flexible than nslookup for gathering performance data and testing DNS servers.

ping is called 'perhaps the most basic tool for internet management'. It verifies that a remote IP implementation and the intervening networks and interfaces are functional, can measure round trip delay, and is based on the ICMP ECHO_REQUEST message. Its caveat is that running it repeatedly could generate high system loads. traceroute discovers the route packets take by relying on the ICMP TIME_EXCEEDED error: it increments the TTL field so that each successive hop can be identified, and it time stamps packets to compute round trip delays. Its caveats note that some IP implementations forward packets with a TTL of 0 and escape identification, and that sending datagrams with the source route option crashes some gateways.

For traffic watching, tcpdump interprets and prints headers for protocols including ethernet, IP, ICMP, TCP, UDP, NFS and ARP/RARP, and has proven useful for examining retransmission and window management in TCP implementations. TTCP and spray are traffic generators: TTCP opens a TCP connection between two hosts and transfers a high volume of data to compute delay and throughput, while spray sends RPC or UDP packets or ICMP Echo Requests and compares packets received with packets sent. Both warn about load: TTCP will greatly increase system load and spray can congest a network.
sections.plainLanguage: Some of the cards are for simple tools. One asks 'are you there?' and times the answer, one shows the path a message takes, and one listens to everything going by on the wire and writes it down.

sections.title: Management Systems, Monitors and Toolkits
sections.content:
A large part of the catalog covers SNMP-based management software. The CMU SNMP Distribution includes source code for an SNMP agent, several SNMP client applications, an ASN.1 library and documentation, and the agent compiles into about 10 KB of 68000 code. Other entries are toolkits, such as the SNMP Application Development Toolkit, a C library for building SNMP applications and agents that is distributed in source form only. Several vendors, including SNMP Research and Empire Technologies, contributed agents, libraries and X-based network management stations such as XNETMON.

Monitoring tools show other approaches. NNStat collects traffic statistics through a promiscuous ethernet tap on each local network rather than by instrumenting gateways: a program called statspy gathers data and a program called collect polls the various statspy processes. NOCOL (Network Operations Center On-Line) is a collection of monitoring agents for Unix systems that record events with four severity levels: CRITICAL, ERROR, WARNING and INFO. nfswatch monitors incoming ethernet traffic to an NFS file server and divides it into categories shown in a continuously updated display.

Not every entry is about packets. The Computer Security Checklist is a DOS program that presents security questions to the user, records the answers and generates a report in which questions are weighted by importance.
sections.plainLanguage: Other cards describe bigger helpers: ones that keep an eye on lots of machines at once, ones that count how busy the network is, and even a quiz program about keeping computers safe.

sections.title: Submitting or Updating an Entry
sections.content:
The catalog is meant to grow, and readers are encouraged to submit new or revised entries for near-immediate electronic publication. The memo gives four steps: review the template to see what information to collect, review the keywords to see the indexing options, assemble or update the entry, and then submit it. A submission can be posted to comp.internet.noctools.submissions or e-mailed to noctools-entries@merit.edu.

New entries are circulated automatically on receipt, and as time permits the NOCtools editors review recent submissions and add them to the master indexes. Questions about the status of a submission go to noctools-request@merit.edu. Submitters should make sure the e-mail addresses in their entries are correct and working, because editors or prospective users may need to reach them.
sections.plainLanguage: If you know a good tool that is missing, you fill in the card and send it in. The editors add it to the list when they have time.

sections.title: The No-Writeups Appendix
sections.content:
An appendix titled No-Writeups collects references to tools that are known to exist but have not been fully cataloged. Anyone willing to write an entry for one of them is asked to contact noctools-request@merit.edu, and tools added later will appear in the on-line catalog. Each mention is separated by a form feed for readability, which readers who print the section may want to strip out.

The mentions are informal. They include a C program called tuecho.c that sends and receives TCP or UDP echoes, a note on SPY, an NFS monitoring and tracing tool, a description of the rpcspy and nfstrace package, and the netck network checker that uses the rstat protocol to collect statistics from machines on the network.

The last catalog entry in the text, for sunsnmpd, is cut off partway through, just before the References.
sections.plainLanguage: At the back is a shelf of tools that people know about but nobody has written a card for yet. The editors ask for volunteers to write them.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The memo says only that security issues are not discussed in it. The catalog does list tools that touch on security. It has a Security keyword for tools that analyze or reduce threats to security, and individual entries carry their own cautions, such as the traceroute warning that source-routed datagrams crash some gateways.

Readers should treat the descriptions as unverified, since the editors state they did not validate most of them.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors did not write a safety chapter. They only warn that they have not tested the tools, so be careful.

items.title: Management area
items.text: The general area or functional role, such as Alarm, Analyzer or Routing.

items.title: Managed resources
items.text: What the tool manages, such as DNS, Ethernet or NFS.

items.title: Mechanism
items.text: How it works, such as SNMP, Ping or Eavesdrop.

items.title: Environment
items.text: Operating system and hardware, such as UNIX, DOS or VMS.

items.title: Acquisition
items.text: Hardware or software release traits, such as Free or Library.

viz.caption: ENTRY TEMPLATE, ABBREVIATED FROM THE RFC

data.title: Catalog entry template
data.code:
NAME
        <tool-name>

KEYWORDS
        [<keyword-A1>[,...]];
        ... (five keyword groups, A to E)

ABSTRACT
        <summary of the tool>

MECHANISM
        <high level technical details of how it works>

CAVEATS / BUGS / LIMITATIONS
        <any warnings or cautions>

HARDWARE REQUIRED
SOFTWARE REQUIRED
AVAILABILITY AND CONTACT POINT FOR INFORMATION ABOUT THIS TOOL
CONTACT POINT FOR CHANGES TO THIS CATALOG ENTRY
DATE OF MOST RECENT UPDATE TO THIS CATALOG ENTRY
        <YYMMDD>
